definition: The field concerned with building systems that perform tasks requiring human-like intelligence.
A subset of AI (Artificial Intelligence) where systems learn patterns from data instead of relying solely on explicit rules.
A type of ML (Machine Learning) that uses labeled data to train models to map inputs to known outputs.
A type of ML (Machine Learning) where the system finds hidden structures or patterns in data WITHOUT labels.
AI (Artificial Intelligence) that is specialized in performing a single task or a limited range of tasks (also called Weak AI (Artificial Intelligence)).
Hypothetical AI (Artificial Intelligence) that can perform any intellectual task a human can across any domain.
A class of AI (Artificial Intelligence) models that can generate new content like text, images, or code from scratch.
When an AI (Artificial Intelligence) system produces unfair results due to historical prejudices in its training data.
The process of anchoring AI (Artificial Intelligence) outputs in verifiable, real-world data sources to reduce hallucinations.
The practice of crafting specific inputs to guide AI (Artificial Intelligence) models toward more accurate or creative outputs.
An error where a generative model confidently produces output that is factually incorrect or nonsensical.
Models capable of processing and generating multiple types of data, such as text, images, and audio, simultaneously.
A learning method where an AI (Artificial Intelligence) explores an environment and receives rewards or penalties to optimize behavior.
A deep learning model trained on vast amounts of text data to understand and generate human-like language.
Providing the AI (Artificial Intelligence) with a task instruction but NO examples of how to perform it.
Including a few examples in the prompt to help the AI (Artificial Intelligence) understand the desired format or task logic.
A core Google AI (Artificial Intelligence) Principle stating that AI (Artificial Intelligence) development should aim to improve people's lives.
A Google AI (Artificial Intelligence) Principle emphasizing the importance of not creating or reinforcing unfair prejudices.
Ensuring that user data protection and privacy are integrated into the AI (Artificial Intelligence) development process from the start.
Google's commitment to rigorous testing and research standards in AI (Artificial Intelligence) development.
Increasing the diversity of training data by creating modified versions of existing data points.
Settings used to control the learning process of an AI (Artificial Intelligence) model, such as 'learning rate' or 'batch size'.
A computing system inspired by the biological brain, consisting of interconnected layers of artificial neurons.
A type of generative AI (Artificial Intelligence) model common in image generation that creates content by reversing a noise process.
A revolutionary neural network architecture that uses 'attention' to process data sequences more efficiently.
Google's most capable family of multimodal generative AI (Artificial Intelligence) models.
Google Cloud service that allows users with limited ML (Machine Learning) expertise to train high-quality models.
Google's platform for building personalized search and conversation experiences using AI (Artificial Intelligence).
Using tools like Gemini or Help Me Organize to automate data classification and analysis.
Using AI (Artificial Intelligence) to condense large documents or email threads into brief, actionable points.
The maximum amount of information (tokens) an AI (Artificial Intelligence) model can 'remember' during a conversation.
When the input data to an AI (Artificial Intelligence) system changes over time, causing the model's accuracy to degrade.
Providing corrupted or misleading input to an AI (Artificial Intelligence) to trick it into performing incorrectly or unsafely.
The ability to understand and describe the internal reasoning of an AI (Artificial Intelligence) model's decision.
Integrating human review and oversight into AI (Artificial Intelligence) workflows to ensure quality and accountability.
The goal of using AI (Artificial Intelligence) to enhance human capabilities rather than replacing people in their roles.
The principle of maintaining control over personal data and digital identity in the age of AI (Artificial Intelligence).
A secure, isolated environment for testing AI (Artificial Intelligence) models and prompts without impacting production systems.
A parameter in generative models that controls the randomness or creativity of the output.
A prompting technique where the AI (Artificial Intelligence) is asked to explain its reasoning step-by-step.
A specialized database used to store and retrieve high-dimensional data (embeddings) for AI (Artificial Intelligence) systems.
The process of a trained AI (Artificial Intelligence) model using its learned knowledge to provide an output for a new input.
A large-scale AI (Artificial Intelligence) model trained on massive datasets that can be adapted to many different downstream tasks.
An enterprise platform for building and scaling AI (Artificial Intelligence) models, including access to Google's specialized hardware.
Breaking a complex task into multiple smaller prompts, using the output of one as the input for the next.
Providing clear information about how an AI (Artificial Intelligence) model was trained, its data, and how it makes its decisions.
The principle that developers and companies are responsible for the outcomes and impact of their AI (Artificial Intelligence) systems.
High-level instructions that define the core personality and safety rules for a generative AI (Artificial Intelligence) model.
A small unit of text (like a word or a syllable) that an AI (Artificial Intelligence) model processes to understand and generate language.
Combining the predictions of multiple AI (Artificial Intelligence) models to create a more robust and accurate overall result.
The examples used to teach a model patterns before it is tested or used in production.
Data held back from training so engineers can estimate how well a model handles new examples.
A separate dataset used during development to compare model versions and tune settings.
An input variable a model uses to make a prediction, such as age, price, category, or word count.
The known answer in supervised learning, such as spam or not spam, that the model learns to predict.
A machine learning task where the model assigns an input to a category or class.
A machine learning task where the model predicts a number, such as cost, risk, or temperature.
An unsupervised learning method that groups similar examples without using predefined labels.
When a model memorizes training data too closely and performs poorly on new examples.
When a model is too simple or poorly trained to capture useful patterns in the data.
A model's ability to perform well on new data that was not part of its training set.
A mathematical measure of how wrong a model's prediction is during training.
An optimization method that updates model weights in the direction that reduces error.
A training setting that controls how large each update to the model's weights should be.
One full pass through the training dataset during model training.
The number of training examples processed before the model updates its weights.
A learned value inside a model, such as a neural network weight, that affects its output.
A model value that controls how strongly one input or neuron influences the next calculation.
A learned value added to a model calculation so predictions can shift up or down.
A function that lets neural networks learn nonlinear patterns instead of only straight-line relationships.
A common activation function that returns zero for negative values and keeps positive values unchanged.
The process neural networks use to calculate how each weight contributed to an error.
A neural network architecture often used for images because it learns local visual patterns.
A neural network designed for sequence data by passing information from one step to the next.
A type of RNN (Recurrent Neural Network) built to remember useful information across longer sequences.
A model technique that lets the system focus on the most relevant parts of the input.
An attention method where each token compares itself with other tokens in the same input.
A numeric representation of text, images, users, or items that captures meaning or similarity.
How close two pieces of content are in meaning, even if they use different words.
A measurement often used with embeddings to compare how similar two vectors are in direction.
The branch of AI (Artificial Intelligence) focused on understanding, generating, or transforming human language.
An NLP (Natural Language Processing) task that identifies names of people, places, companies, dates, and similar entities in text.
An NLP (Natural Language Processing) task that estimates whether text expresses a positive, negative, or neutral attitude.
Assigning text to categories, such as support issue type, topic, urgency, or intent.
Identifying what a user is trying to do from their message or query.
Reducing words to rough root forms, such as running and runner becoming run.
Reducing words to dictionary forms using grammar, such as better becoming good.
Common words such as the, and, or is that are sometimes removed during text processing.
A tool or algorithm that breaks text into tokens a model can process.
Breaking text into pieces smaller than words so models can handle rare or new words more flexibly.
Training a model on broad data before adapting it to a narrower task.
Further training a pretrained model on task-specific data to change or improve its behavior.
Training a model on examples of instructions and desired responses so it follows user requests better.
A training approach that uses human preference judgments to shape model behavior.
A model trained to score outputs according to human preferences or task goals.
The effort to make AI (Artificial Intelligence) systems behave in ways that match human goals, rules, and values.
The field focused on reducing harmful, unreliable, or unintended behavior in AI (Artificial Intelligence) systems.
Testing an AI (Artificial Intelligence) system by deliberately trying to make it fail, break rules, or produce unsafe outputs.
A prompt or technique designed to bypass a model's safety rules or intended restrictions.
An attack where hidden or hostile instructions try to override the intended behavior of an AI (Artificial Intelligence) system.
An attack that corrupts training data so the model learns harmful or misleading patterns.
An attack that tries to infer sensitive training data from a model's outputs or behavior.
An attack that tries to determine whether a specific record was included in model training data.
A privacy method that adds controlled noise so individual records are harder to identify.
A training method where models learn from data across devices or organizations without centralizing the raw data.
Removing or altering personal identifiers so data is less likely to reveal a specific person.
Information that can identify a person, such as name, address, ID number, or email address.
Collecting and using only the data needed for a specific purpose.
Permission from a person or organization to collect, use, or share data under stated conditions.
A measurement used to compare model outcomes across groups and check for unfair differences.
A pattern where a system harms or disadvantages one group more than another, even without explicit intent.
Bias caused when some groups or cases are underrepresented or misrepresented in the data.
Bias caused when the data collected does not accurately measure the thing it claims to measure.
Bias caused when the examples chosen for a dataset are not representative of the real population.
A variable that indirectly stands in for another factor, sometimes exposing sensitive traits by accident.
A table showing correct and incorrect predictions across classes, often split into true and false positives and negatives.
A case where the model correctly predicts that something belongs to the positive class.
A case where the model incorrectly predicts the positive class.
A case where the model correctly predicts that something does not belong to the positive class.
A case where the model incorrectly misses something that belongs to the positive class.
The share of positive predictions that were actually correct.
The share of actual positive cases that the model successfully found.
A metric that balances precision and recall into one score.
The share of all predictions the model got right.
A chart that shows the tradeoff between true positive rate and false positive rate across thresholds.
A single score summarizing how well a classifier separates positive and negative examples across thresholds.
A testing method that trains and evaluates a model across multiple splits of the data.
A portion of data kept separate from training and tuning until final evaluation.
A simple model used as a comparison point to judge whether a more complex model is worth using.
A standard dataset, task, or test used to compare models under similar conditions.
A document that describes a model's intended use, limits, training data, and evaluation results.
A document that explains how a dataset was collected, processed, labeled, and intended to be used.
A record of data, model, prompt, or decision changes that helps teams trace what happened later.
Methods that make AI (Artificial Intelligence) predictions easier for humans to inspect and understand.
A method for estimating which inputs had the most influence on a model's prediction.
An explainability method that estimates how much each feature contributed to an individual prediction.
An explainability method that approximates a complex model near one prediction with a simpler model.
A pattern where a generative model retrieves relevant source material before writing an answer.
The part of a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system that searches for relevant documents or chunks before generation.
Splitting documents into smaller pieces so they can be searched, embedded, or passed into a model.
Reordering retrieved results so the most useful items are placed near the top before generation.
A structured network of entities and relationships that can help systems reason over connected facts.
A model capability where the AI (Artificial Intelligence) returns structured arguments for a tool or API (Application Programming Interface) instead of plain text.
Allowing an AI (Artificial Intelligence) system to call external functions, search tools, databases, or applications to complete a task.
An AI (Artificial Intelligence) system that can plan steps, use tools, and act toward a goal with some autonomy.
Using software or AI (Artificial Intelligence) to run repeatable business steps with less manual effort.
A checkpoint where a person inspects, approves, edits, or rejects an AI (Artificial Intelligence) output.
A defined process for sending uncertain or risky AI (Artificial Intelligence) outputs to a human or higher-control system.
A number that estimates how certain a model is about its prediction, though it may not always be calibrated.
How closely a model's confidence scores match the actual chance of being correct.
A cutoff value used to decide when a model score becomes a positive prediction or action.
Finding unusual patterns or records that differ strongly from normal behavior.
An AI (Artificial Intelligence) system that suggests items, content, or actions based on user behavior and item similarity.
A recommendation method that uses patterns from similar users or items to make suggestions.
A recommendation method that suggests items similar to ones a user already liked.
A model that makes predictions by following a tree of if-then splits.
An ensemble of decision trees whose predictions are combined to improve reliability.
An ensemble method that builds models in sequence, with each one correcting errors from earlier models.
A model that separates classes by finding a boundary with the widest possible margin.
A clustering algorithm that groups data into k clusters by repeatedly updating cluster centers.
A dimensionality reduction method that compresses data while preserving major patterns of variation.
Reducing the number of variables in data while keeping the most useful information.
Rescaling data values to a common range so features are easier for models to compare.
Rescaling values so they have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one.
Representing categories as separate binary columns so models can process them numerically.
Filling in missing data using a rule, statistic, or model-based estimate.
When training data accidentally includes information that would not be available at prediction time.
Artificially generated data used for testing, training, privacy protection, or rare-case simulation.
The process of assigning correct answers, categories, or annotations to training examples.
Instructions that tell human labelers how to label data consistently.
A training strategy where the model asks for labels on examples that would teach it the most.
Reusing knowledge from a model trained on one task to improve performance on another task.
Training a smaller model to imitate a larger model's behavior.
Reducing the precision of model numbers to make the model smaller or faster.
Removing less useful model weights or connections to reduce size and computation.
The time it takes for an AI (Artificial Intelligence) system to return a result after receiving input.
How many requests or examples a system can process in a given amount of time.
Running a trained model behind an application or API (Application Programming Interface) so users can get predictions.
Generating predictions for many records at once instead of responding to one live request at a time.
Generating predictions in response to live user or system requests.
Tracking model quality, inputs, outputs, latency, and errors after deployment.
When the relationship between inputs and correct outputs changes over time.
Running a new model beside the current system without letting it affect real user outcomes yet.
Comparing two system versions with different user groups to measure which performs better.
Rolling out a new model or feature to a small group first so problems can be caught early.
Practices for building, deploying, monitoring, and maintaining machine learning systems reliably.
A sequence of steps that moves data through preparation, training, evaluation, or deployment.
Recording model settings, datasets, metrics, and outputs so training runs can be compared later.
The ability to rerun an experiment or pipeline and get the same or very similar result.
Tracking changes to data, code, prompts, models, or configurations over time.
A model that can work with more than one type of input or output, such as text, images, audio, or video.
A model that connects visual information with language so it can describe, answer, or reason about images.
AI (Artificial Intelligence) that converts spoken language into written text.
AI (Artificial Intelligence) that converts written text into spoken audio.
The branch of AI (Artificial Intelligence) focused on interpreting images, video, and other visual data.
A computer vision task that finds objects in an image and identifies their locations.
A computer vision task that assigns each pixel or region of an image to a class.
A generative model made of two networks: one creates examples and the other judges them.
A generative model that learns a compressed representation and samples from it to create new examples.
A model that generates output step by step, with each new piece depending on earlier pieces.
